<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:moontae.lee@lgresearch.aimoontae.lee@lgresearch.ai">moontae.lee@lgresearch.aimoontae.lee@lgresearch.ai</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) must ensure that retrieved passages are not only individually relevant but also collectively form a comprehensive set.
Existing approaches primarily rerank top-<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> passages based on their individual relevance, often failing to meet the information needs of complex queries in multi-hop question answering.
In this work, we propose a set-wise passage selection approach and introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, which explicitly identifies the information requirements of a query through Chain-of-Thought reasoning and selects an optimal set of passages that collectively satisfy those requirements.
Experiments on multi-hop RAG benchmarks show that <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> outperforms both proprietary LLM-based rerankers and open-source baselines in terms of answer correctness and retrieval quality, providing an effective and efficient alternative to traditional rerankers in RAG systems.
The code is available at <a href="https://github.com/LGAI-Research/SetR" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/LGAI-Research/SetR</a></p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bridging parametric knowledge with external information is vital for ensuring accurate and reliable generation in language models.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) overcomes critical limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly their inability to incorporate up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge without retraining <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mallen et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
The risk of generating hallucinations is another concern when the model capacity is not sufficiently large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
By integrating an external retrieval system that provides contextually relevant and grounded evidence in real time, RAG improves both the accuracy and reliability of knowledge-intensive tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A critical component of RAG systems is the retrieval and reranking module, as the quality of the retrieved information directly influences the accuracy and relevance of the generated answers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2024a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2024b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wadhwa et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
Numerous studies have explored optimizing the effective integration of LLMs and retrieval modules.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asai et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong et al. (2024)</a></cite> focus on dynamically determining the necessity of retrieval and when to stop it.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al. (2023)</a></cite> involve alternating between retrieval and generation, enriching contextual references through multiple retrieval iterations.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarthi et al. (2024)</a></cite> iteratively decompose and refine complex questions, addressing them through retrieval and generation.
However, these multi-step approaches require significantly more resources, potentially limiting their feasibility for real-world applications.
Therefore, many existing RAG systems utilize conventional reranking modules with a straightforward top-k selection strategy, originally developed and optimized for search applications.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2507.06838v2/figures/main_figure_final.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/249;" width="476" height="249" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Overview of our <span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Set selection</span> approach for RAG system, compared to passage reranking methods:
<span id="S1.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a) Direct Reranking</span>, <span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b) Reranking with CoT</span>, and <span id="S1.F1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c) Our <span id="S1.F1.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Set selection</span></span>.
(a) lacks explicit reasoning, making it unclear whether multiple aspects are considered.
(b) incorporates a reasoning process but may misrepresent or underemphasize key information when integrating relevance for final ranking.
(c) <span id="S1.F1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Set selection</span> explicitly identifies all necessary information and selects relevant passages, ensuring more comprehensive information.
This example is from the MultiHopRAG dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang (2024)</a></cite>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We argue that RAG systems have distinct information demands that set them apart from traditional search engines.
While traditional search engines rank individual results by relevance, RAG systems need a curated set of passages to generate accurate answers, requiring not only relevance but also diversity, completeness, and the comprehensiveness of retrieved passages.
For example, when identifying a company based on a mix of business strategies, controversies and product claims, a RAG system must retrieve a diverse range of sources covering all these aspects.
If the system retrieves only passages discussing product claims but not those covering controversies, business strategies, and other relevant factors, it may produce an incomplete or inaccurate response.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we propose a set-wise passage selection approach that optimizes the quality of the passage set as a whole, rather than treating retrieval as an independent ranking task.
This holistic strategy encourages comprehensive coverage of essential information while reducing redundancy within the selected set (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To make it practical for real-world applications, we introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, a fine-tuned LLM designed to implement our set-wise passage selection approach.
The model first analyzes the user question using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to identify its information requirements, and selects an optimal subset from the full list of retrieved passages, maximizing coverage and relevance. This enables our method to serve as an effective alternative to rerankers in RAG systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Experiments on multi-hop RAG benchmarks, including HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultiHopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, MusiQue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and MultiHopRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang, 2024</a>)</cite>, demonstrate that set-wise passage selection significantly enhances the effectiveness of RAG systems. It outperforms both proprietary LLM-based reranking and open-source rerankers, achieving higher answer correctness.
Moreover, retrieval performance evaluation on MultiHopRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang, 2024</a>)</cite> indicates improvements in precision and recall, further underscoring its strong retrieval capabilities even in isolation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The ablation study of <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> reveals that the performance boost stems from both the set-wise passage selection approach and CoT reasoning for identifying information requirements, each making a distinct and effective contribution to retrieval quality.
The analysis shows that both components enhance information coverage in the retrieved set while effectively rejecting negative candidates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The contributions of this work are threefold:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Set-wise Passage Selection for RAG:</span> We propose an information requirement-based set-wise passage selection approach that ensures collective coverage of retrieved passages, optimizing the retrieved set as a whole rather than treating retrieval as an independent ranking task.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comprehensive Evaluation of Set Retrieval and Generation:</span> To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive evaluations on both the retrieved passage sets and the final generated outputs. Our experiments on multi-hop RAG benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms both proprietary LLM-based rerankers and open-source alternatives, achieving better answer correctness, while also improving retrieval precision and recall.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Open-Source Contribution:</span> We release the complete and fully reproducible recipe of <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, implementing our set-wise passage selection approach. We hope this work facilitates future research and communty-driven advancements in retrieval strategies for RAG systems.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems combine retrieval modules with language models to enhance factual accuracy and reduce hallucinations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewis et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guu et al. (2020)</a></cite>.
Standard pipelines typically employ a first-stage retriever such as BM25 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robertson and Zaragoza (2009)</a></cite> or DPR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpukhin et al. (2020)</a></cite> followed by a reranking module that estimates relevance via pointwise, pairwise, or listwise strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nogueira and Cho (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoon et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been applied to listwise reranking in RAG systems through prompting and distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pradeep et al. (2023b)</a></cite>, demonstrating strong performance.
However, these models primarily focus on individual passage relevance and often overlook set-level properties such as diversity or coverage, which are crucial for generating complete and accurate answers in multi-hop or compositional question answering tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Refinement and Iteration in RAG</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address the limitations of ranking-based retrieval, recent studies have explored retrieval strategies better aligned with the needs of RAG.
These include adaptive retrieval based on query complexity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong et al. (2024)</a></cite>, multi-step reasoning with agent-based ranking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and context pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chirkova et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Iterative methods such as Self-RAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asai et al. (2023)</a></cite> and CoRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024)</a></cite> refine queries or perform multi-round retrieval to improve relevance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While effective, these approaches often entail substantial computational overhead and are sensitive to prompt design and hyperparameter choices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asai et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
In contrast, our study provides a lightweight and efficient alternative by selecting a coherent subset of passages in a single step through explicit modeling of information requirements.
This set-oriented approach is compatible with iterative retrieval pipelines and can also function as a direct replacement for conventional rerankers in standard RAG systems.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> (<span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Set</span>-wise passage selection for <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">R</span>etrieval-Augmented Generation), a novel retrieval paradigm that moves beyond conventional reranking strategies.
We begin by formalizing the passage selection task and motivating the need for a set-oriented perspective (§<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Task Definition ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).
Next, we present our information requirement identification (IRI) method, which utilizes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to guide passage selection (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Information Requirement Identification via CoT Reasoning ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).
Finally, we describe the architecture and training methodology of <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, a distilled model fine-tuned for efficient set-wise passage selection (§<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), along with the data construction details (§<a href="#S3.SS3.SSS1" title="3.3.1 Data Construction ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.1</span></a>) and training procedures (§<a href="#S3.SS3.SSS2" title="3.3.2 Training ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Task Definition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define the passage retrieval task as the process of selecting an optimal set of passages from a pool of retrieved candidate passages to address a specific information need, such as supporting precise and coherent responses in RAG systems. Traditionally, this task has been framed as a reranking problem, where passages are scored individually and the top-<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> results are selected based on their relevance scores.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, we argue that relevance-based reranking alone is insufficient for retrieval modules in RAG systems, which require more holistic retrieval strategies.
To address this, we propose a set-wise retrieval approach that jointly optimizes the relevance, completeness, and conciseness of the retrieved set. This method also eliminates the need to manually select the top-<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> value in reranking, streamlining the process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Information Requirement Identification via CoT Reasoning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design a prompting strategy that enables set-wise passage selection by systematically identifying information requirements through a structured, step-by-step reasoning process.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3.2 Training ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, our prompt guides a zero-shot CoT reasoning process that decomposes the input question into distinct information subgoals.
The key process consists of three key steps:
(1) enumerating the key information requirements necessary to answer the question;
(2) identifying passages that contain relevant information for each requirement; and
(3) selecting a subset of passages that collectively provide the most comprehensive and diverse coverage to effectively answer the query.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">By prompting Large Language Models (LLMs) with both the question and a set of candidate passages retrieved in an earlier retrieval stage, this method enables fine-grained analysis and effective set selection.
In contrast to zero-shot listwise reranking, our approach imposes no constraint on the inclusion of all candidate passages and does not enforce any ranking or ordering in the final selection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Model Distillation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the proposed approach is practical for real-world applications, we train <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, a distilled model fine-tuned for the set-wise passage selection task through information requirement identification. While proprietary LLMs exhibit strong performance, their cost and latency would make their use in real-time search systems impractical.
Instead, we distill step-by-step reasoning ability into a specialized, lightweight model for efficiency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>Data Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For distillation, we construct a dataset based on 40K training questions<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/castorini/rank_zephyr_training_data" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/datasets/castorini/rank_zephyr_training_data</a></span></span></span> from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pradeep et al. (2023b)</a></cite>, originally derived from the MS MARCO v1 passage ranking dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Each query is paired with the top-20 retrieved candidate passages.
We then apply set-wise passage selection to generate teacher-labeled selections, which are subsequently distilled into our student model.
To perform this labeling, we use GPT-4o with a zero-shot prompting approach.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pradeep et al. (2023a)</a></cite>, we replaced all instances of [n] in passages with (n) to prevent model confusion during data synthesis and inference.
We used the fix_text function from ftfy<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              <a href="https://pypi.org/project/ftfy" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://pypi.org/project/ftfy</a></span></span></span> to preprocess all inputs before feeding them into the model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Training</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct<a href="#footnote5" title="footnote 5 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> as the base model and train it using a standard supervised fine-tuning approach.
The input consists of a prompt including the user question and retrieved passages, while the output includes the CoT reasoning from the teacher model along with the selected passages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the ablation study, we present two additional model variations. We refer to the original model as <span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT &amp; IRI for comparison with these variations. Full prompt details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Prompt Templates ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>.</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR<span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">-Selection only</span></span> is a model trained to generate only the final selected passages without any reasoning process.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR<span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">-CoT</span></span> is a model trained with general CoT reasoning using a standard “Let’s think step-by-step prompt” prompt, but does not explicitly identifying distinct information requirements.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR<span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">-CoT &amp; IRI</span></span> is the full model that incorporates both CoT reasoning and explicit information requirement identification, and performs passage selection accordingly.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.F2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="243.11" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 653.15 243.11" width="653.15"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,243.11) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 237.21 C 0 240.47 2.64 243.11 5.91 243.11 L 647.24 243.11 C 650.51 243.11 653.15 240.47 653.15 237.21 L 653.15 5.91 C 653.15 2.64 650.51 0 647.24 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 205.09 L 651.18 205.09 L 651.18 5.91 C 651.18 3.73 649.42 1.97 647.24 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 210.99)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:44.07em;--ltx-fo-height:1.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="26.21" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 26.21)" width="609.8"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first introduce the experimental setup (§<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). Then, we show the results for both the generation (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) and retrieval stages (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Retrieval Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>. More details are shown in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Appendix ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmarks</span>. For evaluation, we conduct experiments in two folds: (1) end-to-end QA, and (2) retrieval task.
For comprehensive evaluation, we adopt four widely used complex multi-hop QA datasets: HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultiHopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al. (2020)</a></cite>, MuSiQue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al. (2022)</a></cite>, and MultiHopRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang (2024)</a></cite>.
These datasets cover diverse question types and multi-hop reasoning scenarios, offering a comprehensive evaluation of QA models in complex, real-world contexts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines</span>.
We compare <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> with state-of-the-art ranking baselines across different model categories. Specifically, we include traditional unsupervised ranking models such as BM25 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robertson and Zaragoza (2009)</a></cite>, supervised dense ranking models including bge-large-en-v1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and bge-reranker-large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2023)</a></cite>, as well as LLM-based ranking models such as RankLlama <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2024)</a></cite>, RankVicuna <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pradeep et al. (2023a)</a></cite>, RankZephyr <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pradeep et al. (2023b)</a></cite>, FirstMistral <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2024)</a></cite> and RankGPT (<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">4</span></span>
                
                
                
              <span id="footnote4.6" class="ltx_text">gpt-4o</span><span id="footnote4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> refers to </span><span id="footnote4.8" class="ltx_text">gpt-4o-2024-08-06</span><span id="footnote4.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> from OpenAI</span></span></span></span></span>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details</span>. <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> is built upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct<a href="#footnote5" title="footnote 5 ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, trained for 5 epochs with an effective batch size of 512 and a learning rate of <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> using AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter (2019)</a></cite>.
To evaluate the effectiveness of <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>, we keep the first-stage retrieval and the generator fixed. The first-stage retrieval uses bge-large-en-v1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2023)</a></cite>, a high-performance retrieval model, while the generator is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct</a></span></span></span> which we use without fine-tuning.
For RAG, we adopt the standard RAG framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ram et al. (2023)</a></cite> to generate answers based on the retrieved contexts.
All baselines are implemented utilizing the Rankify <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdallah et al. (2025)</a></cite> toolkit<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/Rankify" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/Rankify</a></span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>End-to-end QA Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The main results of various ranking models are presented in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3.2 Training ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
The results in <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Retrieval Only</span> are derived solely from first-stage retrievers, while <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reranking</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Set Selection</span> correspond to the results of re-ranking or selecting over the top-20 candidates retrieved by the respective first-stage retrievers.
Based on the results, the key observations are as follows:
(1) In terms of answer correctness, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> significantly outperforms all baselines by selecting the optimal set of passages from the retrieved passages, achieving notably higher F1 and Accuracy.
These results are quite impressive, considering that <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> uses 40-50% fewer passages on average compared to baselines.
(2) The performance of LLM-based ranking baselines, such as RankLlama and RankZephyr, was less satisfactory. We observe that the relatively small bge-reranker-large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al. (2023)</a></cite> performs comparably to, and in some cases even outperforms LLM-based baselines.
This is likely due to complex questions making retrieval more challenging, introducing more noise, and requiring not only relevance but also diversity, completeness, and comprehensiveness.
We posit that the key to the RAG system lies in having more useful knowledge and fewer distracting passages, enabling even a simple and smaller model to outperform LLMs when the correct RAG paradigm is applied, which we will discuss in detail in (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Effectiveness of Set Selection: Informativeness and Robustness ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Retrieval Evaluation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The retrieval evaluation is conducted using both rank-based metrics such as MRR and NDCG, as well as presence-based selection metrics including Precision and Recall, on the MultiHopRAG dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Yang (2024)</a></cite>.
The results of retrieval evaluation are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Retrieval Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
The results indicate that our model consistently achieves 3.8%-4.6% higher precision compared to off-the-shelf baselines, whereas it maintains competitive performance on rank-based metrics even with a small number of passages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">LLM-based rankers, paired with advanced retrievers, perform well on rank-based metrics compared to the first-stage retrieval baselines.
Specifically, RankGPT (<span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o</span>) shows notable improvements in both rank-based and presense-based metrics.
However, we observe a discrepancy between rank-based metrics and end-to-end QA performance, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3.2 Training ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>
Retrieval performance on the MultiHopRAG benchmark. <span id="S4.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Rank-based</span> metrics reflect passage order, while <span id="S4.T2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Presence-Based</span> metrics consider only presence. Best and second-best scores are in <span id="S4.T2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bold</span> and <span id="S4.T2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underlined</span>, respectively.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This discrepancy arises from the assumption in rank-based metrics that relevance is determined on a one-to-one basis between a document and a query.
For more complex question types, such as multi-hop questions, where considering relationships between multiple documents is needed for comprehensive information retrieval, these metrics may need further refinement to improve accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Analysis</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze the key components that contribute to the effectiveness of our set-wise passage selection approach <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>.
We evaluate the quality of selected passages in terms of information coverage and robustness (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Effectiveness of Set Selection: Informativeness and Robustness ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>), assess the impact of reasoning strategies including information requirement identification (IRI) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Effectiveness of Reasoning Components: The Role of CoT and IRI ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, design a controlled setup to isolate method-level effects (§<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>), and compare token efficiency between selection-based and reranking-based methods (§<a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Efficiency Analysis ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Effectiveness of Set Selection: Informativeness and Robustness</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the effectiveness of our selection approach in terms of two key perspectives: (1) informativeness; how comprehensively the selected passages cover the necessary information, and (2) robustness; the model’s ability to discard irrelevant or redundant content.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Informativeness</span>.
Traditional ranking-based retrieval systems typically score and select passages based on their individual relevance rather than the collective information gained from multiple passages, and often fail to account for content duplication.
To address this, we additionally analyze <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">information coverage</span>, measuring how <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">newly</span> retrieved gold evidence accumulates as the number of selected documents increases.
This helps capture how <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">valid</span> information accumulates as additional documents are included.
The MultiHopRAG dataset provides gold evidence lists, extractively collected from documents, allowing precise measurement of how much necessary information is covered by the selected passages.
The formula used to calculate information coverage is detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Additional Experimental Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.
We report two complementary metrics: Hit@<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">k</span>, which reflects whether gold evidence appears in the top-k selected passages, and <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">information coverage</span>, which measure the accumulation of distinct gold evidences across the selected evidences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf1" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf4" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(d)</span></a>,
despite <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> selects passages without any ordering, it outperforms reranking methods with a notable improvement at Hit@<span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">k</span> from 48.87% to 69.90%.
Furthermore, <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> enhances information coverage from 19.33% to 36.49%, whereas other rerankers achieve only a modest average gain of 9.80% in the acquisition of new information.
These findings suggest that reranking methods may struggle to retrieve documents containing previously uncovered information due to the presence of duplicate content and hard negatives.
In contrast, our method captures both individual relevance and collective information coverage, which are essential for improving retrieval effectiveness and overall answer correctness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness</span>.
We further assess the robustness of our approach to retrieval noise by analyzing how answer generation quality changes as the number of passages increases.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf2" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(b)</span></a>, <a href="#S4.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(c)</span></a>, <a href="#S4.F3.sf5" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(e)</span></a>, and  <a href="#S4.F3.sf6" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 End-to-end QA Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(f)</span></a>, simply increasing the number of input passages often leads to performance degradation, suggesting that more is not always better.
This is especially pronounced in multi-hop QA, where irrelevant or contradictory evidence can mislead the generator.
In contrast, <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> consistently achieves stronger performance while utilizing significantly fewer passages.
On average, it uses 2.91 passages compared to the standard top 5 used in reranking.
This demonstrates the model’s ability to discriminate high-utility information from distractors, thereby maintaining both efficiency and factual precision.
These findings suggest that effective passage selection requires balancing recall and conciseness, and that a smaller, curated set can outperform longer, noisier contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Effectiveness of Reasoning Components: The Role of CoT and IRI</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the role of reasoning in passage selection, we conduct an ablation study with three <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> variants: (1) without any reasoning, (2) with general CoT reasoning, and (3) with our proposed IRI-based reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As presented in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3.2 Training ‣ 3.3 Model Distillation ‣ 3 SetR: Set-wise Passage Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Retrieval Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
in terms of precision, we observe a significant performance improvement when applying IRI-based explicit requirement analysis and selection, compared to using standard CoT reasoning alone, or no reasoning process.
Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows a similar trend, applying IRI-based reasoning yields stronger end-to-end RAG performance compared to other methods; more details are in §<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.
These results suggest that the performance gains of our approach do not simply stem from leveraging the intrinsic thinking steps of LLMs, and highlight the critical role of our IRI step in assembling a passage set with maximum information coverage, demonstrating the best performance across all metrics and benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While prior sections demonstrate that our approach improves end-to-end performance, such comparison can still be influenced by external factors, including differences in base models, data sources, or teacher supervision.
To more rigorously assess the intrinsic effectiveness of our set-wise selection approach, we conduct a method-level evaluation that explicitly controls for these confounding factors.
Specifically, we implement two strategies to minimize the impact of confounding factors: (1) upper bound; a teacher model directly performs the selection task, to isolate the contribution of the method itself,
and (2) unified setting; all baselines are retrained using the same base model, training data, and teacher supervision, ensuring a fair and method-focused comparison.</p>
</div>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>
Ablation study with teacher model inference to isolate method-level effects. All experiments use <span id="S5.T3.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-2024-08-06</span> as the reference model, annotated with <sup id="S5.T3.10" class="ltx_sup">⧫</sup>. For <span id="S5.T3.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reranking</span>,
RankGPT4 prompt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>
is employed. Prompts for <span id="S5.T3.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Set Selection</span> are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Prompt Templates ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>. <span id="S5.T3.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2Wiki</span> and <span id="S5.T3.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MHRAG</span> refer to the 2WikiMultiHopQA and MultiHopRAG benchmarks, respectively.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Teacher model as Upper Bound.</span>
We first design an upper-bound evaluation setup where all models, whether reranking or selection-based, leverage the same powerful teacher model, GPT-4o, to generate passage selections or ranking.
This setup isolates the effect of the selection formulation itself by minimizing the influence of model capacity or training-specific artifacts.
Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, which reports the method-level effects with teacher model, indicates that our set selection method outperforms traditional reranking strategies, highlighting the individual contributions of both CoT reasoning and IRI to enhanced retrieval performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, the <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> method with IRI consistently achieves strong performance across all benchmarks and demonstrates competitive or superior results compared to both traditional reranking and other set selection variants.
Notably, while both Rank + CoT and <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT share the same CoT prompt, the results reveal that using set-wise selection rather than integrated ranking in the final stage leads to improved retrieval outcomes.
This suggests that constructing a unified ranking may lead to the omission of certain aspects of the reasoning process, potentially resulting in information loss.
Furthermore, the comparison between <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT and <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT &amp; IRI demonstrates that explicitly identifying essential information during the reasoning process helps improve selection precision and ensures broader information coverage.</p>
</div>

<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S5.T5.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:72.1pt;vertical-align:-34.7pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-145.9pt,30.5pt) scale(0.541706167711912,0.541706167711912) ;">
<table id="S5.T5.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T5.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></th>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Efficiency analysis on token usage. We report the number of output tokens generated during retrieval and the number of input tokens fed into the generator, both of which serve as proxies for computational efficiency.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unified Setting for Direct Comparison.</span>
To further minimize potential bias, we create a unified training setting, in which all models are (1) built on the same base architecture (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), (2) trained on the same teacher supervision (re-annotated with <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-2024-08-06</span>), and (3) evaluated using identical generation protocols.
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> again surpasses reranking baselines in end-to-end QA accuracy across all tasks, reaffirming the advantages of selection-based approaches.
This carefully controlled comparison highlights a critical insight: ranking-based reasoning, even with CoT, tends to collapse multiple reasoning chains into a single score, potentially obscuring key informational elements.
In contrast, our selection strategy preserves intermediate reasoning steps, resulting in better alignment with the actual information needs of the question.
These findings collectively demonstrate that the observed performance gains stem not from stronger base models or teacher supervision alone, but from our methodological reformulation of retrieval as set selection grounded in reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Efficiency Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An ideal retrieval method for RAG systems should not only achieve strong performance—yielding accurate results—but also be efficient, minimizing latency, memory usage, and compute cost for real-world deployment.
While direct measurement of GPU time or inference latency depends on hardware and implementation choices, token-level analysis offers a practical proxy for computational efficiency.
We compare token usage across models by measuring: (1) the number of input tokens passed to the generator, and (2) the number of output tokens generated during the retrieval stage.
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.3 A More Equitable Comparison: Method-Level Effects ‣ 5 Analysis ‣ Shifting from Ranking to Set Selection for Retrieval Augmented Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, all <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> variants require substantially fewer input tokens than reranking-based methods.
For instance, on MultiHopRAG, <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT &amp; IRI feeds only 1,240 input tokens into the generator, compared to 2,672 in RankZephyr.
Despite this sharp reduction, <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> not only maintains answer quality but often surpasses reranking models in F1 and accuracy.
Interestingly, even within <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> variants, reasoning plays a role in efficiency. <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-Selection only is the most efficient in terms of token usage, while <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span>-CoT &amp; IRI trades some marginal increase in prompt length for greater answer correctness and recall.
This suggests a useful accuracy-efficiency trade-off spectrum that practitioners can tune based on resource constraints and latency budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work highlights the limitations of conventional top-<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems and proposes a set-wise passage selection approach to better address the unique information needs of generative models. By incorporating information requirement identification and Chain-of-Thought reasoning for passage selection, <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> (<span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Set</span>-wise passage selection for <span id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">R</span>etrieval-Augmented Generation), enhances retrieval precision and improves end-to-end answer accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A promising direction for future work is enabling efficient selection from large candidate passage pools (e.g., 100 passages). Unlike traditional listwise reranking, which often relies on sequential sliding windows, our approach supports parallel, order-agnostic selection—reducing time complexity and improving scalability.
Additionally, future work could explore how <span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">SetR</span> iteratively refines queries for better retrieval and develops adaptive selection techniques to adjust the number of selected passages based on domain-specific needs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our set-wise passage selection approach improves retrieval quality and efficiency in RAG systems, it has several limitations.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, our method relies on a predefined retrieval pipeline, meaning its performance is still dependent on the initial retrieval stage. If the initial retrieved set lacks critical information, even an optimal set-wise selection cannot compensate for missing knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Second, our method optimizes retrieval for multi-hop and complex queries but has not yet been validated across diverse RAG domains such as code generation or conversational AI. While we anticipate broader applicability, further evaluation on diverse tasks is needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Lastly, our approach relies on the quality of the underlying language model for reasoning-based selection. While chain-of-thought reasoning improves passage selection, its effectiveness depends on the LLM’s ability to accurately analyze and synthesize information.</p>
</div>
</section>
